samples.brief: Faceless YouTube Shorts script for a Hindi personal-finance and history channel ('Paisa Kahani'): how India pledged its gold in 1991 to avoid defaulting; VO in Hindi (Devanagari) for a TTS voice, visual and on-screen-text columns in English; 45-60 seconds (about 110-150 words of VO); every line paired with an archival or AI-generated visual description; goal: viewer watches to the payoff and follows for part 2.

Title: 1991: जब भारत ने अपना सोना गिरवी रखा
Columns: No. | VO (Devanagari, for TTS) | Visual (shot) | On-screen text | SFX / music | Seconds.

- 47 tonnes, July 1991, roughly 400 million dollars: RBI and Bank of England records of the July 1991 gold shipment [verify exact tonnage and amount against the RBI Annual Report 1991-92 before publishing].
- Reserves covering about three weeks of imports in mid-1991: RBI and Economic Survey 1991-92 figures [verify the exact reserve number and import cover].
- Gulf War oil shock and fall in remittances: Economic Survey 1991-92 [verify].
- Rupee devaluation (early July 1991) and the New Industrial Policy (24 July 1991) ended most industrial licensing: Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Statement on Industrial Policy 1991 [verify dates].
- Gold was pledged, not sold, and redeemed within months [verify the redemption date in RBI records].
- "Hundreds of billions of dollars" of reserves today: latest RBI weekly statistical supplement [replace with the current figure and date].
- Synthetic elements: AI voice-over (yes, TTS), AI-generated visuals (yes: shots 1, 6; stylised graphics elsewhere), no real person's face or voice, no fake archival footage presented as real. Disclosure: on-screen text "AI-generated visuals and voice" at 0-3 s, YouTube altered/synthetic content setting ticked, description line "AI se banaye gaye visuals aur voice-over".
- TTS notes: numbers are written as words (सैंतालीस, चालीस करोड़), no abbreviations, each line is one breath; listen back to the first word of lines 3, 6 and 10 for clipping.

FACT CHECK

No, Bihar has not announced a free scooty for every Class 10 girl from January 2027

[Demo note: every [source placeholder] below marks a document or call this draft could not open. Fill each with the real finding and link before publishing, and change the rating if a finding differs.]

We found no budget line, scheme page or order for a scooty scheme open to every Class 10 girl, and the department's spokesperson said no such scheme exists [spokesperson quote placeholder]. The claim is False.

HOW WE CHECKED

1. Read the state budget speech. We opened the Bihar Budget speech for 2026-27 [source placeholder: link to the speech PDF] and searched the full text for "स्कूटी", "scooty", "two-wheeler" and "Class 10" in the girls' education sections. samples.brief: Question-led article for a Jaipur CA firm's website: 'GST registration for Etsy and Amazon sellers in Rajasthan: 8 questions answered'; audience: home-based craft sellers doing Rs 5-40 lakh a year; English with Hindi terms where sellers use them; 900-1,300 words; each H2 a real client question with a 1-2 sentence answer first; one worked example from the firm's (anonymised) client files; goal: reader books a Rs 999 registration consult.
samples.text:
GST registration for Etsy and Amazon sellers in Rajasthan: 8 questions answered

Selling craft items from your Rajasthan home on Etsy or Amazon? "Do I need GST?" has no single answer. It depends on what you ship, where it goes and which platform you use. These are the eight questions home sellers ask us most, each answered in the first lines, with the detail after. Rules are as we last checked them on [date]; where a rule has conditions we have marked it [verify] for our CA reviewer.

1. Do I need a GST number to sell on Amazon from Rajasthan?

In most cases, yes. Amazon asks for a GSTIN (your GST number) for most product categories, and the GST law requires registration for goods sold through an e-commerce platform unless a specific exemption applies (see question 3).

Open Seller Central's registration page for your exact category before you start [verify category-wise], because a few categories onboard without one. If you plan to sell more than one category, plan on registering once and being done: the GSTIN belongs to you, not to the platform.

2. What is the turnover limit for GST registration in Rajasthan?

Rs 40 lakh a year for a seller of goods, Rs 20 lakh for a service provider [verify current limits]. But that limit rarely protects an online seller, because ship-to-another-state sales and platform rules switch registration on earlier.

The limit counts all your sales together: Amazon, Etsy, Instagram orders and walk-in customers, under one PAN. It also includes exports. For example, a seller may count only Rs 6 lakh of Etsy payouts and miss Rs 14 lakh sold on Amazon and Instagram. Her real turnover is Rs 20 lakh.

3. Can I sell only inside Rajasthan on Amazon without registering?

Possibly. A 2023 notification lets small sellers who supply goods only within their own state through an e-commerce platform stay unregistered, if their total turnover is under the limit above [verify: Notification 10/2023-Central Tax].

In practice the platform decides. Amazon's own onboarding may still ask for a GSTIN, and the moment one order goes to another state, the exemption stops. A first order from a buyer in Delhi in month three is enough to end it.

4. I ship to customers in other states. Does that force registration?

For goods, yes: an inter-state supply needs registration regardless of turnover. The one narrow exception is for handicraft goods when your turnover is below Rs 20 lakh [verify: Notification 56/2018-Central Tax and its conditions].

That exemption is easy to overestimate. It covers listed handicraft goods only, and a platform that demands a GSTIN overrides it in practice. We check each client's product list line by line before relying on it.

5. I sell to buyers abroad on Etsy. Do I need GST for exports?

You charge no GST to a foreign buyer, because exports are zero-rated. But to export without paying IGST you need a GSTIN and a Letter of Undertaking (LUT), and exporting goods usually also needs an Import Export Code [verify for your courier or postal route].

With a GSTIN you can also claim back the GST you paid on inputs such as fabric, packaging and courier. Without one, that GST is simply a cost of doing business.

6. What documents do I need to register?

You need five things. PAN and Aadhaar of the owner. A passport-size photo. Bank account proof: a cancelled cheque or the first page of the passbook. Address proof for the place of business. A mobile number and email for OTPs.

If you work from your home, use the electricity bill or property tax receipt. If the house is owned by a parent or in-law, you also need a consent letter from them and a copy of their address proof. Have your Etsy shop name ready: it can go on the certificate as your trade name.

7. How long does GST registration take, and what does it cost?

The government charges no fee. Approval is due in 3 working days if you complete Aadhaar authentication, 7 otherwise, but a query from the officer restarts the clock [verify against CGST Rule 9].

Queries usually come from an address proof that does not match the form, or a name that differs between PAN and bank. Fix both before you apply, not after the query arrives.

8. What happens after I register? Which returns do I file?

You file GSTR-1 (your sales) and GSTR-3B (your tax payment) every month, even in months with zero sales [verify whether quarterly filing applies to you]. The composition scheme is not open to sellers who supply goods through e-commerce platforms.

Amazon deducts a small tax (TCS) from your payouts and shows it in your GST ledger. You claim it when you file. Unclaimed TCS is money left sitting in your ledger.

FROM OUR CLIENT FILES

[Client case, anonymised: a block-print home seller in Jaipur. Platforms: Etsy and Amazon. Annual turnover: Rs [X] lakh. Registered in [N] working days. Result: [client result: e.g. LUT filed, first refund claim of Rs [Y]]. Add the one thing she did not expect, in her words if she agrees.]

NEXT STEP

Not sure where you stand? Book our Rs 999 registration consult at [booking link]. Bring your PAN, a list of the products you sell and the states you ship to, and we will tell you in one call whether to register now, wait, or use an exemption.

Written by [author name], [firm name]. Reviewed by [CA name, membership no.]. Last updated [date].

samples.text:
Ghanavali FAQ: your questions about our cold-pressed oils

Short answers on purity, delivery and returns. Jump to: Product & purity | Orders & delivery | Returns & payments.

PRODUCT & PURITY

What does "cold-pressed" actually mean?
It means the seeds are pressed slowly at low temperature, with no chemical solvent and no refining afterwards. The oil keeps its natural colour, smell and taste. Our press temperature stays below [X degrees C], and you can see the process on our [How we press page link].

Is it 100% pure, with nothing mixed in?
Yes. Each bottle holds one oil only: no blending with cheaper oil, and no added colour, flavour or preservative. Every batch is tested at [lab name and accreditation], and you can read the report for your bottle's batch number at [batch report link]. Our FSSAI licence number is [FSSAI no.].

Why does it cost more than the oil at my kirana store?
Cold pressing gives less oil from the same quantity of seed, and we do not refine, bleach or deodorise to stretch it. You pay for a lower yield and a cleaner process, not for a label. A 1-litre bottle costs Rs [X] and works out to about Rs [Y] per month for a family of [N].

Can I use it for everyday cooking, including tadka and frying?
Yes for tadka, sabzi, parathas and shallow frying. For deep frying, use [oil name] and keep the temperature moderate [confirm smoke-point guidance per oil]. Switching oils is fine; start with one dish and see how the taste suits your family.

Why is there sediment, or cloudiness, at the bottom?
Because the oil is unrefined. Tiny seed particles settle over time and are harmless. Coconut oil, if you order it, also turns solid in cool weather and melts again when the bottle sits in warm water for a few minutes. Neither means the oil has spoiled.

How long does it last, and how do I store it?
Use it within [X months] of the pressing date printed on the bottle. Keep it away from the stove and direct sunlight, and close the cap tightly after each use.

ORDERS & DELIVERY

Do you deliver to my pin code?
Enter your pin code on any product page and it tells you at once, before you add anything to the cart. We currently deliver to [N] pin codes across [states/regions]. If yours is not covered, write to us and we will tell you when it may be.

How many days will delivery take?
[X-Y] working days to metro pin codes and [A-B] working days elsewhere. Orders ship from Pune within [Z] working days, and you receive a tracking link by WhatsApp and email.

Is cash on delivery available?
Yes, for orders up to Rs [X] on eligible pin codes, with a COD fee of Rs [Y] shown at checkout before you pay. Pay online by UPI and the fee does not apply.

Will the bottle leak on the way?
It should not. Every bottle is sealed, wrapped and packed in [packaging detail]. If one still reaches you leaking, see the next section: we replace it.

RETURNS & PAYMENTS

What if the bottle arrives damaged or leaking?
Send us a photo or short video within [X hours/days] of delivery on WhatsApp at [number], and we replace the bottle or refund you, your choice, within [X working days]. You do not pay for the return.

What if I do not like the taste or smell?
Cold-pressed oil smells and tastes stronger than refined oil, and that is normal. We cannot take back an opened bottle for taste alone, because oil is a food product [confirm policy]. If you are unsure, order the [small size] first at Rs [X].

How do refunds work?
Refunds go back to the original payment method within [X-Y] working days of our approving them. For COD orders, we ask for a UPI ID or bank details and refund there.

Which payment methods do you accept?
UPI, debit and credit cards, net banking and cash on delivery [confirm list]. Payments are processed through [payment gateway name], and we do not see or store your card details.

STILL STUCK?
Message us on WhatsApp at [number], [days], [hours] IST. We reply within [X hours]. Or email [email]; we answer within [X working days].

samples.brief: Brand-journalism feature for the blog of a Jaipur handicraft export house: how a third-generation blue-pottery artisan in Kot Jewar village moved half her sales to Instagram orders; audience: design-conscious buyers in India and abroad; English; 1,000-1,300 words; quotes come from a supplied interview (demo: write the interview notes first and label them as notes); goal: the reader finishes and clicks through to the artisan's collection.
samples.text:
DEMO INTERVIEW NOTES (invented for this sample so the feature has a source; replace with the real interview notes before publishing)
Subject: Sunita Devi Prajapat, 41, blue-pottery maker, Kot Jewar village, Jaipur district. Interviewed at her home workshop on [date].
Observed: she paints a plate at a low table by the courtyard door; her phone is propped against a steel jug, filming her hand.
Family: her grandfather learned the craft; her father made [item types]; she began at 12. She works with her mother-in-law and two women from the village. Daughter Pooja, 19, studies BCom.
Process, her words: no clay, the body is quartz stone powder, glass powder, multani mitti and gum. Shaped in a mould, dried, painted with cobalt, glazed, fired once at about 800 degrees.
Quote 1: "Dadaji kehte the, ye mitti nahi hai, patthar ka aata hai. Isliye isme sabr lagta hai."
Quote 2: "Pehle plate dukaan mein 600 ki bikti thi, mujhe 200 milte the."
Quote 3: "Pooja ne ek video daala. Main bas plate paint kar rahi thi. Teen din baad Bengaluru se ek madam ka message aaya."
First order, as she remembers it: 12 coasters and 2 vases for a Bengaluru cafe owner.
Quote 4: "Last year ke hisaab se aadhi bikri Instagram orders se aayi. Baaki mela aur dukaan se."
Quote 5: "Phone raat ko bhi bajta hai. Pehle sirf mela mein baat hoti thi."
Quote 6: "Ek order mein 14 mein se 2 piece tut gaye. Ab main har order mein do extra bhejti hoon."
Quote 7: "Bazaar mein machine wali blue pottery 150 mein milti hai. Customer ko samjhana padta hai ki mera glaze haath se hota hai."
Quote 8: "Shop wale 200 dete the. Ab usse zyada milta hai, kitna, ye nahi bataungi."
Pooja: answers messages after college and keeps the order sheet in a school notebook, columns ruled by hand: name, city, pieces, colour, date promised.
Quote 9: "Wo type jaldi karti hai, main paint achha karti hoon."
Pricing: she now sets her own prices and sends a short video to any buyer who finds them high; she now says in her videos that the glaze is hand-done; she packs each order herself.
Observed, 9 am: the plate is set on a rack, cobalt still dark and matte; she checks four messages and writes a number on the back of her hand.
Outside voice: [craft-trade expert or a Kot Jewar potter who stayed with the shop, name and source to add before publishing].
Order desk coordinator, [export house, name to confirm]: orders now come mostly as sets of 6 to 24 matching pieces for cafes and homes; buyers write asking for the maker, not the brand.

---

One plate at a time: how a Kot Jewar potter moved half her sales to Instagram

At seven in the morning, Sunita Devi Prajapat sits at a low table by her courtyard door in Kot Jewar, painting a cobalt vine along the rim of a white plate. Her phone leans against a steel jug, filming her hand. A leaf takes her three strokes. Before she finishes the second one, the phone buzzes. She does not look up.

She has learned that most buzzes can wait for the leaf.

Sunita is a third-generation blue-pottery maker in the village outside Jaipur that has given the craft its best-known address. For years the money in her work went to the shop that stocked it. Last year, by her own count, half of her sales came from people who found her on Instagram and ordered directly. "Last year ke hisaab se aadhi bikri Instagram orders se aayi," she says. "Baaki mela aur dukaan se." Her story is about what happens when a craft with a long chain of sellers gets a short line to its buyer, and what that line asks of the person at the other end of it.

A stone, not a clay

The first thing she tells visitors is that the plate in front of them contains no clay. Jaipur blue pottery is made from quartz stone powder, glass powder, multani mitti and gum, shaped in a mould, dried, painted in cobalt, glazed and fired once at about 800 degrees, she says. Her grandfather used to put it more simply. "Dadaji kehte the, ye mitti nahi hai, patthar ka aata hai. Isliye isme sabr lagta hai."

That patience is why one plate takes days, and why for most of her working life she could not price it fairly. She began at 12. Her mother-in-law and two women from the village now work beside her, and the courtyard is lined with plates in each stage: white, painted, glazed, fired.

Rs 600 in the shop, Rs 200 in her hand

Until a few years ago, Sunita's pieces left Kot Jewar in two ways: through a Jaipur shopkeeper, and through an annual fair where she met buyers face to face. The shop was reliable and set the terms. "Pehle plate dukaan mein 600 ki bikti thi, mujhe 200 milte the," she says. The buyer in the shop never learned her name.

The change did not start with a plan. Her daughter Pooja, 19, who studies BCom, filmed her mother painting a plate and posted it. Sunita remembers the sequence plainly. "Pooja ne ek video daala. Main bas plate paint kar rahi thi. Teen din baad Bengaluru se ek madam ka message aaya." The first order was for 12 coasters and two vases for a cafe owner there. Sunita priced it herself.

Pooja has since become the other half of the business. She answers messages after college and keeps the order sheet in a school notebook, its columns ruled by hand: name, city, pieces, colour, date promised. The division of labour suits them both. "Wo type jaldi karti hai, main paint achha karti hoon," Sunita says, and goes back to the rim of the plate.

The export house's order desk has watched the pattern repeat since. Orders now arrive mostly as sets of six to 24 matching pieces for cafes and homes, and buyers write asking for the maker, not the brand, the desk coordinator says. People who want a plate, it turns out, also want to know whose hand painted the vine.

What the phone costs

None of this has been free. The first cost is sleep and attention. "Phone raat ko bhi bajta hai. Pehle sirf mela mein baat hoti thi," she says. A fair is a few days a year. A message can arrive at 11 at night, from a buyer who would like to know if the blue can be a shade deeper.

The second cost is breakage. Blue pottery is glazed and brittle, and a courier does not care. In one early shipment, two pieces of 14 arrived broken. "Ek order mein 14 mein se 2 piece tut gaye. Ab main har order mein do extra bhejti hoon." The extras are a cost she absorbs, and she packs each order herself.

The third is comparison. A buyer scrolling past her page sees blue plates at a fraction of her price, and some of them are machine-made. "Bazaar mein machine wali blue pottery 150 mein milti hai. Customer ko samjhana padta hai ki mera glaze haath se hota hai." She now says it in the videos themselves, over the sound of the brush.

Not every family in Kot Jewar has followed her online, and the picture is not simple. [Outside voice to add: a craft-trade expert, or a Kot Jewar potter who stayed with the shop, on whether Instagram suits every maker, with name and source.] Sunita herself does not want the platform to replace the older routes. The fair and the shop still carry the other half of her sales.

What the platform has changed is who sets the price. She now quotes her own rates and, when a buyer finds one high, sends a short video of the work. samples.brief: Treatment (900-1,200 words) for an 8-episode Hindi OTT thriller pitched to a Mumbai production house: a Varanasi boat-owner's daughter discovers her father's ghat business is laundering election cash; English prose (any dialogue lines in Roman Hindi); includes logline, four character sketches, the season arc in three acts and the ending.
samples.text:
GHAAT KA HISAAB
8-episode Hindi OTT series | political thriller | approx. 45 minutes an episode | set in Varanasi

LOGLINE
When a boat-owner's daughter, a young accountant, finds that her father's ghat business is washing a party's election cash, she must either bury what she knows to keep her family or use her ledgers to bring down the man who owns the river's money.

CHARACTERS

Gauri Sahani, 24. She wants to turn her father's fourteen boats into a clean, modern business and prove that a boatman's daughter can keep books better than any firm in town. Her flaw is that she trusts numbers over people. She stands to lose her father and the name Sahani carries on the ghats.

Ramnath Sahani, 55. A boatman who built a fleet from one hired oar. He wants his daughter safe and his debts gone, and he has been paying for both with a favour he has not told her about. His flaw is silence. He stands to lose Gauri's respect.

Brijesh Tiwari, 46. The party's man on the ghats. He wants Rs 40 crore of cash converted into clean money before polling day, because his boss has told him to. His flaw is that he believes loyalty is a currency. He stands to lose everything if one wad goes missing.

Aman Rai, 29. A flying-squad officer posted from Lucknow for the bypoll. He wants a big seizure to save a career stalled by a past refusal to look away. His flaw is impatience. He stands to lose his posting, and his belief that the law can reach this far.

ACT ONE (Episodes 1-2)

Gauri returns from her articleship in Lucknow for Dev Deepawali, the week the ghats earn most of their year. Cleaning up her father's accounts, she finds a boat that was in dry dock logging Rs 11 lakh of fares in a single night. It is impossible, so she checks the other thirteen. Eleven show the same pattern: cash arriving on the boats that carry no passengers.

She does not go to the police. She goes to her father. Ramnath tells her it is a tourist boom, and when she shows him the dry-dock receipt, he finally admits Brijesh "uses the ghat for the party's convenience." He says it is only until the polls. But Brijesh has already noticed that the ledger has been opened. He visits the house with sweets. His message is warm and unmistakable: "Ghat par sab bikta hai, Gauri. Sirf kinara nahi."

She decides to stay and quietly copy every page, because only she understands how the money moves. Episode 2 ends with Aman's flying squad arriving on the ghat, and Gauri hiding a photographed ledger inside an aarti plate.

ACT TWO (Episodes 3-6)

Gauri finds out how the system works: cash enters as boat fares, puja-samagri sales and guesthouse bookings, then exits as GST-paid invoices. Brijesh, meanwhile, has seen her skill. He offers her a job, "Munim ki jagah", and threatens her father if she refuses. So she accepts, planning to learn the full chain. In episodes 3 and 4 she becomes his accountant, and it works: she sees the boss's name for the first time, a sitting minister's brother-in-law.

But the work makes her complicit, and the first fracture comes with Aman. He raids a boat at midnight in episode 4, which is the midpoint. He finds the cash, and because Gauri has been steering the route, the boat is Ramnath's. Ramnath takes the blame so she can stay inside. He is arrested.

Now Gauri must choose between freeing him by confessing, and finishing the case. Aman, who knows more than he says, offers a deal: help me, and I will help your father. She refuses, afraid of Brijesh's reach. In episode 5 she moves the cash herself, one more time, to protect her father in custody.

The low point comes in episode 6. Ramnath is released on bail, but Brijesh burns her hidden ledger, transfers Aman out of the district, and tells her the boss now has a copy of every sheet she touched. Her father tells her to leave Varanasi. She has no proof, no ally, and her own signature on every page.

ACT THREE (Episodes 7-8)

But Gauri has one thing the powerful have never counted: the boatmen. Each boat keeps a daily handwritten tally slip, a parchi, and she has kept every slip for six months in her father's old tin trunk. They are the only record that cannot be burned, because two hundred families keep their own copies. Ramnath understands at once what they are.

So she goes from boat to boat and shows the boatmen how they have been used. The Nishad community, who have worked the river for generations, agree to move one more shipment, the biggest, on the night before polling, with Gauri and Ramnath guiding it. In episode 8 the cash travels across the river on thirty boats during the evening aarti, each wad photographed and logged. Brijesh watches from the ghat, believing he is winning. Aman, back from his transfer, waits on the far bank with the squad.

THE ENDING

The squad seizes the cash on the far bank. Brijesh is arrested on the steps of the ghat. The minister's brother-in-law is named in the records but is never charged, and the bypoll goes ahead the next morning. Ramnath pleads guilty to a lesser charge and serves fourteen months. Gauri is not charged, since the tally slips and her testimony prove she acted under threat. She does not leave Varanasi.

In the last scene she runs the boats as a cooperative owned by the boatmen. She opens a new ledger, and writes the first line: her father's name, and what he owes the river.

Client: [name], 32, Surat, third generation. Family shop "[family name] Sarees" in the Ring Road textile market, opened by his dada in [year].
Papa runs the counter and keeps the hisaab by hand in a red-cloth ledger: one pen behind his ear, one in his hand. He never forgets a figure he has written. Sells mostly wholesale to agents from Mumbai and Hyderabad. Udhaar of 45 to 60 days is normal. Nobody shouts over a price; both sides know it before the first word.
Dada's rule, painted over the counter: "Hisaab chokho, vaat saachi." The shop's name board outside was hand-painted in dada's time and has faded. The client sat at the counter on weekends after college.
At 2 am Mummy comes to the stairs with a glass of milk. He shows her the page. She says: "Itna sundar? Humne banaya?" He does not tell her the price.
The client's own words and phrases: "maal", "chokho hisaab", "dikra" (what Papa calls him), "sheth", "Chalo, joiye" (let's see), "Kaai nai" (never mind), "yaar".
Diwali 2019: the shop is jammed, agents' tempos double-parked outside, tea going cold on the counter. Papa sells 40 georgette sarees with a peacock border to a Mumbai agent. Agent offers Rs 620; Papa says Rs 650 and offers tea; agent pays Rs 650. The client helps load the tempo and thinks it was a good day.
In September the same batch had arrived with a weaver's slip: one feather off-centre in the pallu. Papa noticed, shrugged: "Kaai nai. Customer ko pata nahi chalega."
Around 11 that night, shutters down, the client sits on the stairs outside and scrolls Instagram. He sees the same saree, same peacock border, same off-centre feather, on a Mumbai boutique page at Rs 3,200. A model laughs in a doorway.
He does the maths twice, thumbnail on the back of his hand: Rs 2,550 more per saree, Rs 1,02,000 on the 40.
At 2 am he orders one at Rs 3,200 by UPI and feels a little sick when it goes through.
It arrives in 5 days in tissue paper, tied with ribbon, with a handwritten card: "Thank you for choosing us. We hope it feels as special to wear as it was to make." He sits on the floor of his room and reads it three times. He has been in the room where it was made; nobody there ever said anything like that.
Sunday morning, shop empty, fan turning, a sweeper working down the lane. He puts his phone in front of Papa. Papa studies it, finds the feather: "Haan. Wahi hai. Pallu dekho. Wohi galti." Client: "Rs 3,200." Papa, not looking up: "Dikra. Maal bechna mera kaam hai. Naam bechna dusron ka kaam hai."
The client stops talking and waits. Papa turns a ledger page back, then forward, twice. Then: "Chalo, joiye." "Kitna time?" Client: one month, ten sarees, he takes the photographs and writes the cards himself, and pays for the ten if it fails. Papa taps the red ledger twice with his pen: it means the matter is entered.

---

CHAPTER ONE: RS 650

The night I found out what we were really selling, I was sitting on a staircase with my thumb on a phone, and the shop below me was dark.

Earlier that day I could not have reached the cash drawer. It was Diwali 2019, and our shop in the Ring Road market had done what it does every Diwali: filled up. Agents' tempos were double-parked outside. Bundles were stacked to the ceiling. Tea was going cold on the counter because nobody had a free hand to pick it up.

If you are the first in your family to run a business, you may not know how a shop like ours keeps its books. Ours has a red-cloth ledger, one pen behind Papa's ear and one in his hand, and a sentence painted over the counter in dada's time: "Hisaab chokho, vaat saachi." Clean accounts, true word. We sell mostly wholesale, to agents from Mumbai and Hyderabad, and the agents pay in 45 to 60 days. That is udhaar. It runs on memory and trust, and Papa has never lost either.

I sat at that counter on weekends after college. I thought I understood the business.

That day Papa sat at the counter in his usual spot with the red ledger open in front of him. Every sale goes into that ledger first and into his head second. I have never seen him write down a figure he did not remember later.

That afternoon, a Mumbai agent bought forty georgette sarees with a peacock border. The agent said Rs 620. Papa said Rs 650 and offered him tea. The agent took the tea and paid Rs 650. That is how it goes in our market. Nobody shouts over a price, because both sides know it before the first word is spoken.

I helped load the bundles into the tempo. I remember thinking it had been a good day.

Around 11 that night, the shutters were down and I sat on the stairs outside, tired, scrolling Instagram with no purpose. And I saw a saree.

Georgette. Peacock border. A model in a doorway, laughing. It was a beautiful picture, and the saree looked familiar the way your own handwriting looks familiar on a card you do not remember writing.

I zoomed in on the pallu. Near the edge, one feather sat slightly off-centre. I knew that feather. Our weaver had made that slip in the whole batch we received in September. Papa had noticed it, shrugged, and said, "Kaai nai. Customer ko pata nahi chalega."

The customer had not noticed. The customer had paid Rs 3,200.

I did the maths with my thumbnail on the back of my hand, the way Papa taught me. Rs 3,200 minus Rs 650 is Rs 2,550. I did it again, because I did not trust my thumb. Rs 2,550, on one saree. Forty sarees. Rs 1,02,000.

A lakh and two thousand rupees had left our shop that afternoon in a tempo, and I had helped to load it.

I did not sleep. Around 2, Mummy came to the stairs with a glass of milk and found me staring at the phone. I turned the screen towards her. She looked for a long time and said, "Itna sundar? Humne banaya?"

I did not tell her the price.

At 2 in the morning I did something I had never done in my life. I opened a stranger's page and bought a saree from my own family's stock. Rs 3,200, by UPI. When the payment went through, I felt a little sick.

*

The box came five days later.

I had handled that saree forty times at the shop. In bundles, tied with jute, thrown into a tempo. This was not that. This was tissue paper, folded carefully, tied with a ribbon. On top there was a small card, and on the card somebody had written by hand: "Thank you for choosing us. We hope it feels as special to wear as it was to make."

I sat on the floor of my room and read it three times.

As it was to make. I had been in the room where it was made. Nobody in that room had ever said a sentence like that card, and nobody at our shop ever had either.

That was the whole difference, and it took me a long time to see how big it was. The saree that left our shop carried a price and nothing else. The saree that left their page carried a face, a name, a ribbon and a card. The saree was the same. What the customer was buying was not.

Mummy's question from the stairs came back to me. Humne banaya? We had. And nobody on the other end was ever going to know.

In our market, a customer who is unhappy goes to the agent, and the agent comes to Papa. A customer who is happy goes nowhere. We had never once been thanked by the person who wore our work, because that person did not know we existed. For forty sarees in one afternoon, I could not name a single woman who owned one.

Our name was nowhere. I thought of the board outside the shop, hand-painted in dada's time, its letters faded now to the colour of weak tea. Nobody outside our market ever reads it.

Forty sarees, forty homes, and not one woman who would ever know they came from a shop on Ring Road that has been selling cloth for three generations. Our work was real. It was just invisible.

*

I told Papa on Sunday morning.

The shop was empty. A fan was turning overhead. Outside, a sweeper was working his way slowly down the lane. I had practised what to say. I decided to start with the number, because Papa believes in numbers, and I put my phone down in front of him with the boutique's page open.

"Papa. This is our saree."

I had expected anger, or an argument, or a lecture about how the shop had fed our family for three generations. I got something harder to deal with. He picked up his glasses, bent over the screen, and zoomed in with two fingers, the way I had. He found the feather.

"Haan. Wahi hai. Pallu dekho. Wohi galti."

"Rs 3,200," I said.

He did not look up. "Dikra. Maal bechna mera kaam hai. Naam bechna dusron ka kaam hai."

That was the sentence of a man who has done one thing well for forty years and does not need his son to tell him it is not enough. It was also, I think now, the sentence of a man who was a little afraid. Where I come from, fear and pride can sound exactly alike.

I did not argue. I know what happens when you push Papa: the ledger closes. So I did what I had watched him do to a stubborn agent. I stopped talking, and I waited.

He turned a page of the red ledger back. Then forward. Then back again. I have since learned what that means. It means he is counting something that is not written in the book.

"Chalo, joiye," he said.

"Papa?"

"Kitna time?"

I had not practised this part. "One month. Ten sarees. I take the photographs myself, I write the cards myself, and if it fails, I pay for the ten. Not the shop."

Papa picked up his pen and tapped the red ledger twice. It is a very small thing. In my family it means that the matter has been entered.

That is how I got ten sarees and one month.

If you are building something from nothing, with no red ledger and no board painted by your grandfather, you will still meet your own version of that Rs 2,550. It is the gap between what you make and what the person at the other end knows you made. I had been standing on one side of that gap for twelve years without seeing it, because everyone around me stood on the same side and nobody ever looked across.

Papa's sentence was not wrong. It was complete, for the world he grew up in. In that world, a trader's reputation lived in the market, among agents who knew him, and it paid him in the only way it needed to: Rs 650, on time, every time. What he could not see from the counter was that a customer in a doorway in Mumbai had no idea there was a Papa at all.

That is the idea this book is built on, and I only half understood it that morning. I understood it enough to ask for ten sarees. I had no idea what I was doing. Chapter Two starts with the first of those thirty days.

[ASK CLIENT before Chapter Two: which ten sarees did you pick, who photographed them, and what happened on day one?]

samples.brief: Glossary entry 'What is a UPI AutoPay mandate?' for the help hub of a Bengaluru subscription-billing SaaS; audience: D2C founders setting up subscription plans; English; 300-500 words; worked example with a Rs 499-a-month plan; links to 2 related entries and the product's mandate-setup guide; goal: the reader understands the term and clicks to the setup guide. samples.text:
What is a UPI AutoPay mandate?

A UPI AutoPay mandate is a one-time instruction, approved with a customer's UPI PIN, that lets a business collect recurring payments from their bank account up to an agreed amount and schedule. For a subscription business, it means customers pay each month without opening their UPI app.

How it works

1. At checkout, the customer chooses UPI AutoPay. Your payment gateway sends a mandate request to the customer's UPI app.
2. The app shows your business name, the amount, how often you will collect (for example, monthly), and the start and end dates.
3. The customer approves it once with their UPI PIN. The mandate now exists.
4. Before each debit, the customer's bank or UPI app sends a pre-debit notification [verify the notice period required by the current RBI and NPCI rules].
5. On the due date, you trigger the debit through your gateway. The money moves if the account has enough balance and the amount is within the mandate.
6. The customer can pause or cancel the mandate from their UPI app at any time. After that, you cannot collect.

You can set a fixed amount (Rs 499 every month) or a maximum amount, if the bill varies from month to month [verify which options your gateway supports]. There is also a per-debit limit; debits above it need the customer to approve each one [verify the current limit and any higher limits for specific categories].

Worked example

Neha subscribes to your Rs 499-a-month plan on 5 March. She approves a mandate for Rs 499, monthly, for 12 months. On 4 April, her UPI app notifies her that Rs 499 will be debited on 5 April. On 5 April, you trigger the debit and the money arrives in your account. The same repeats on 5 May, and every month after.

In month 4, her account balance is Rs 300 and the debit fails. You see the failure status in your dashboard and send her a reminder to top up [verify retry rules]. If she cancels in her app after month 6, you have collected Rs 2,994 and the remaining six debits will not go through. Over the full 12 months, a Rs 499 plan is worth Rs 5,988 to you.

Related terms

UPI AutoPay is often confused with eNACH. Both set up recurring debits. eNACH is registered against a bank account through net banking or a debit card. UPI AutoPay is approved inside a UPI app with the UPI PIN [verify the current differences before publishing]. See also: [What is eNACH?], [What is a pre-debit notification?], [What is involuntary churn?].

Next step

Ready to set it up for your plans? Follow [our UPI AutoPay mandate-setup guide], which walks you through creating the plan, the mandate request and the retry settings.

CSR CONCEPT NOTE
Women Solar Pump Technicians: 300 women, 12 villages, 2 years
Submitted by [NGO name], Jaipur, to [Company] CSR Foundation
Budget requested: Rs 48,00,000 over 24 months

1. SUMMARY

[NGO name] requests Rs 48 lakh over 24 months to train 300 women in 12 villages around [Company]'s [plant location], [district], to install-check, maintain and repair solar water pumps. Each woman gets a 10-day course, a toolkit and 12 months of mentoring. A pump that breaks today waits for a technician from [nearest town], often for weeks. By the end of the programme, every one of the 12 villages will have a trained local repair team. At least 180 of the 300 women (60%) will be earning from repair work six months after their training, up from none today [baseline to be confirmed in month 3]. The programme falls under Schedule VII of the Companies Act, 2013 (rural development, vocational skills and women's empowerment), and serves the local area around the plant.

2. NEED

Water in these villages increasingly depends on solar pumps. In [district], [X] solar water pumps are installed across [N] villages [source: state or district records, year]. These pumps stop for simple reasons: dust on the panels, a loose connection, a failed controller, an air-locked pump. Repair needs a technician, and the nearest trained one is [distance] km away [source: village survey, year]. In the 12 villages, pumps stay out of service for an average of [baseline: days] [source: our baseline, to be collected]. During that time, women and girls carry water from [source].

The need is also about work. Only [X]% of rural women in [district] are in paid work [source: NFHS-5 or PLFS, year]. Solar pump repair is a skill that the village needs every month, that does not require a woman to leave home, and that no one in the village currently offers. To our knowledge, no programme in [district] trains women in pump repair [confirm after a scan of local NGOs and the District Skill Committee].

3. OBJECTIVES AND OUTCOMES

Objective 1: Build a trained local repair workforce. Objective 2: Get pumps repaired faster. Objective 3: Create a repeatable income for women.

Indicator | Baseline | Target | By
Women who complete the 10-day course (output) | 0 | 300 | Month 12
Trained women who pass the practical test (output) | 0 | 270 (90%) | Month 12
Trained women earning from pump repair six months after training (outcome) | 0 [confirm] | 180 (60%) | Month 24
Average days a pump stays out of service, in the 12 villages (outcome) | [days, from baseline] | Half of baseline | Month 24
Average monthly repair income of an active woman technician (outcome) | Rs 0 | Rs [target to be set from baseline] | Month 24

4. APPROACH AND TIMELINE

We train in the village, on the village's own pumps, so that the skill and the customer are in the same place. Each village forms a 25-woman cohort chosen with the panchayat, with priority for women from households without a regular income [selection criteria to be agreed with the Foundation].

The 10-day course covers six things. Safety on a roof and around electrical connections. Reading a pump's fault signs. Testing panels, controllers and wiring with a multimeter. Cleaning and re-fixing panels. Priming and testing pumps. Keeping a repair record and a rate card. Each cohort learns on a practice pump unit kept in the village, then repairs real faults under the trainer's supervision.

After training, a woman works in a pair, and every pair is linked to the village committee and a local solar vendor for parts and warranty cases. Repair calls route to a WhatsApp number, so a pump owner can reach a nearby technician without a phone call chain. Women charge a visit fee set with the panchayat [Rs X per visit, from baseline].

Risks and how we handle them. Families may not allow women to climb roofs or visit other homes, so village committees and the women's families are involved from month 1. Pump models differ, so the trainers learn each village's installed models before training and add them to the course. If a woman drops out, a waitlisted woman from the same village takes her place.

Workplan (24 months)
Months 1-3: recruit staff, select villages and cohorts, form village committees, baseline survey.
Months 4-12: run 12 cohorts of 25 women, one village at a time by two technician-trainers.
Months 5-24: mentoring visits for each cohort for 12 months after its training, with refresher days at months 6 and 12.
Months 22-24: endline survey, learning review with the Foundation, handover to village committees.

5. ORGANISATIONAL CAPACITY

[NGO name] has worked in [N] villages of [district/state] since [year]. [Track record: two or three projects with numbers and dates, for example women trained, income outcomes, grant sizes.] The team has four people. A project coordinator [name, background]. Two technician-trainers [names, certificates, years of solar experience]. A finance lead [name]. We will work with [solar vendor or ITI partner] for course certification and parts supply. Registrations: 12A [no.], 80G [no.], CSR-1 [no.], PAN [no.], audited accounts for the last 3 years (Annexure).

6. MONITORING AND EVALUATION

Each indicator in Section 3 has an owner. Attendance and test results are recorded by the trainers on a phone form at every session. Repair jobs are logged by the women on a simple record card; the field team verifies 1 in 5 against the pump owner. Pump downtime is measured by a short survey of owners in all 12 villages at baseline (month 3) and endline (month 22). Income is self-reported and cross-checked against the repair log. We will send the Foundation a short quarterly report and a full learning review at month 24 [reporting format to be agreed].

7. BUDGET AND JUSTIFICATION

Line | Unit cost and quantity | Amount (Rs)
Project coordinator | 24 months x Rs 30,000 | 7,20,000
2 technician-trainers | 24 months x 2 x Rs 17,500 | 8,40,000
Toolkits | 300 women x Rs 3,000 | 9,00,000
Trainee travel and meal support | 300 women x 10 days x Rs 300 | 9,00,000
Practice solar pump units | 12 x Rs 25,000 | 3,00,000
Training consumables and spares | 12 villages x Rs 20,000 | 2,40,000
Village mobilisation and committees | 12 x Rs 10,000 | 1,20,000
Baseline and endline surveys, monitoring | Lump sum | 3,00,000
Mentoring and refresher visits, field travel | 24 months | 2,40,000
Administration and audit (5%) | Lump sum | 2,40,000
Total | | 48,00,000

[Unit costs to be confirmed against current vendor quotes before submission.] The toolkit is the largest single item, because a woman who owns her tools can start working the week she finishes. Travel and meal support lets women from poorer households attend 10 days without losing wages. Two technician-trainers are enough for 12 cohorts, because the cohorts run one after another. Administration is 5% of the grant.

8. SUSTAINABILITY AND EXIT

After month 24, the programme's costs are small: parts, travel and a phone line. These are covered by the repair fees women charge, with a small share going to a village repair fund held by each committee. Each village committee keeps its own practice pump and the rate card. The solar vendor has a reason to keep supplying parts, because the women bring it repeat orders [confirm in a written understanding with the vendor]. We will ask each panchayat to pass a resolution adopting the repair team [to be confirmed with panchayats]. [NGO name] will stay in contact for a further 6 months on its own funds [confirm] to resolve any disputes.

ANNEXURES
Registration certificates (12A, 80G, CSR-1); audited accounts for 3 years; letters of support from panchayats and [solar vendor]; CVs of key staff; village list with locations; monthly workplan.

samples.text:
How to cut COD return-to-origin (RTO) orders: 4 fixes from the D2C brands we work with

Every D2C founder in India knows the sinking feeling of an RTO. The parcel went out, the courier tried, the customer refused or never picked up, and the box came back. You paid the forward shipping, the return shipping and the packing. You got nothing.

Here is what that costs on a small scale. Take illustrative numbers, not a client report: a brand ships 1,000 COD orders a month and 30% come back. If each RTO costs Rs 155 in shipping both ways plus packing, that is 300 x Rs 155 = Rs 46,500 a month, before counting the sales you did not make.

The brands we work with have found that RTO is rarely one problem. It is four, and each has a different fix. Here they are, in the order we would try them.

1. Confirm the order before you ship it

Many COD orders are placed on impulse. The customer clicked "Cash on Delivery" because it felt risk-free, then forgot, changed their mind, or entered a number they do not answer.

The cheapest fix we have seen is a confirmation message right after the order. On WhatsApp or SMS, the customer gets: "Your order of [product], Rs 799, will be shipped tomorrow. Reply 1 to confirm, 2 to cancel, or change your address here." Orders that get no reply in a set window, say 12 hours, are held, not shipped. A phone call to the held orders from a human can recover many of them.

Illustrative example: a skincare brand with 1,000 monthly COD orders starts holding unconfirmed orders. About 15% are never confirmed. The brand ships 850, not 1,000, and the RTO rate on shipped orders falls from 30% to 22%. It ships fewer orders and loses fewer rupees. The numbers are made up to show the logic; your own data will say what your brand's number is.

What to avoid: confirming by a single message and treating silence as a yes. Silence is the signal.

2. Treat pin codes and addresses as data, not as text

Not every address is equal. Some pin codes, in some cities, return much more often than others. A COD order to an incomplete address ("near the temple, Sector 5") is a coin toss.

Pull your last three months of orders and sort them by pin code. A spreadsheet is enough. Export three columns: pin code, payment mode, final status (delivered or RTO). Make a pivot table of COD orders and COD RTOs per pin code. Ignore any pin code with fewer than 20 orders, because the sample is too small to judge. Rank the rest by RTO rate.

You will usually find that a small number of pin codes cause a large share of your RTOs. Check this on your own data before you act on it.

For the worst pin codes, you have three choices. You can allow COD only above or below a certain order value. You can ask for a small advance payment. Or you can offer prepaid only. For the good pin codes, keep COD as it is.

Also fix the address form. Make the landmark field required, match the pin code to the city, and block obviously incomplete entries such as a single word.

3. Give people a reason to pay online

The most reliable way to cut COD RTO is to have fewer COD orders. But nobody likes being forced, so offer something in exchange.

A small prepaid benefit works better than a lecture: Rs 50 off, free shipping, or a free sample. Some brands go the other way and add a COD fee of Rs 40 to 50 shown at checkout before the customer pays. Both work. Test one at a time, because changing two things makes the result unreadable.

A middle path is partial COD: the customer pays Rs 100 by UPI to confirm the order and the rest on delivery. That Rs 100 is the customer's proof of intent, and it covers a good part of your shipping loss if the order still comes back.

Be honest about the offer. If you show "Pay online and save Rs 50" and then add the amount back in a fee later, customers notice, and refunds and complaints follow.

4. Fix what happens after the courier fails

Not every RTO is the customer's fault. Courier attempts fail because the rider could not find the house, called a wrong number, or tried once and gave up. Many couriers send a "non-delivery report" (NDR) to you when an attempt fails, and many sellers answer it too late or never.

The brands that do this well treat the NDR as a 24-hour job. When an attempt fails, the customer gets a WhatsApp message in minutes: "Our delivery partner could not reach you today. Reply with a good time tomorrow or share a landmark." Your support team forwards the reply to the courier as a re-attempt request.

Check your courier's NDR rules too: how many attempts it makes, how long it waits, and when it returns the parcel [link: your courier's NDR policy page]. Then compare couriers by zone. One courier may be strong in metros and weak in smaller towns, and you can route accordingly.

Where to start

Do not try all four at once. Start with confirmation messages, because they are the cheapest and show results in days. Then rank your pin codes. Then test one prepaid offer. Then clean up your NDR process.

Measure RTO by pin code and by courier, before and after each change, and give each change two weeks. If a change does nothing, drop it. If it works, keep it and move on to the next.

An RTO is not bad luck. It is information about an order that was wrong in a specific way: the wrong customer, the wrong address, the wrong payment method or the wrong courier. Find which one, and it gets cheaper to fix.

[HERO]
Homes and haveli hotels designed for Jaipur's light, heat and heritage

Studio Haveli Modern is a Jaipur architecture and interiors studio. We design 2,000 to 5,000 sq ft homes and boutique hotels in converted havelis.

[Book a free 30-minute site visit]   [See our projects]

[PROBLEM AND VALUE]
A Jaipur house has to handle May afternoons, a monsoon week and a family that gathers for every festival. A haveli has to survive a conversion without losing what made you buy it. Most plans handle one of these and forget the others.

We start from the site: where the sun falls, where the wind goes, what the walls can carry. Then we draw the plan, and the interiors follow from it. You get a building that is comfortable in summer and looks like the drawings.

[TWO PATHS]
Building a home in Jaipur? You own a plot or an old house, and you want 2,000 to 5,000 sq ft that suits your family. See how we design homes. [link]

Converting a haveli into a boutique hotel? You own an old haveli and want to open rooms without losing its character or its permissions. See how we convert havelis. [link]

[HOW IT WORKS]
1. Free site visit (30 minutes). We walk the plot or the haveli with you, and listen to what you want it to do.
2. Concept and plan. You see layouts, a material palette and a fee quote before you commit to the next stage [fee model, confirm].
3. Drawings and approvals. We prepare drawings for the local approvals your project needs [confirm: JDA or other authority].
4. Build and interiors. We visit the site through construction and design interiors that fit the plan.

We take few projects at a time, so the architect you meet at the site visit is the one who draws your plans [confirm]. Our principal architect is registered with the Council of Architecture, [CoA no.].
